gospel.d: ‘Good news’ (Greek euangelion). In the New Testament it means the announcement of what God has done in Jesus Christ: his death for our sins, his resurrection, and his reign as Lord (1 Corinthians 15:1–5), with the call to repent and believe. All Christian traditions agree on this core. They differ on how a person receives what the gospel offers (see justification, faith).

grace.d: God’s undeserved favour and kindness, given freely and not earned. In Paul it is the opposite of wages (Romans 4:4; 11:6): salvation is a gift from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9).

v.t: Grace is God’s sovereign kindness. For those he saves, God’s grace does not merely make salvation possible but actually brings them to faith. The Spirit effectively draws them to Christ, ‘yet so as they come most freely’ (Westminster Confession 10.1).
Grace goes before every person (‘prevenient grace’), freeing the will enough to respond to God. Without it no one can turn to God, but it can be resisted (Remonstrance, 1610, art. 4).

Grace is both God’s favour and a real gift of new life poured into the soul (‘sanctifying grace’), first given in baptism and nourished through the sacraments. It can be lost through grave sin and restored through penance.

justification.d: God’s act of declaring a person ‘righteous’, that is, in the right with him and accepted. It is a law-court word: the opposite of condemnation (Romans 8:33–34). Paul’s central claim is that we are justified by grace, through faith in Christ, not by doing what the law requires (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28).

v.t: A once-for-all legal verdict. God pardons all our sins and accepts us as righteous, not for anything done in us, but by counting (‘imputing’) Christ’s obedience and death to us, received by faith alone. The inner change of sanctification always follows but is distinct (Westminster Confession 11.1).
The same Reformation teaching: we are freely justified for Christ’s sake through faith, not by our own merits or works (Augsburg Confession, art. 4).

Justification is by grace through faith alone. Wesley wrote: ‘The plain scriptural notion of justification is pardon, the forgiveness of sins.’ Faith is the condition God has appointed for receiving it.

Justification is ‘not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man’. It is first given in baptism, can grow, and can be lost and restored. Nothing before justification, whether faith or works, earns it (Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 7–8).

works-of-the-law.d: Paul’s phrase (Galatians 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10; Romans 3:20, 28) for doing what the law of Moses requires. Paul insists no one is justified this way. The phrase also appears in a Dead Sea Scroll (4QMMT), so it was real Jewish vocabulary of the time.

v.t: Obedience to the whole law, moral as well as ceremonial, as a basis for being accepted by God (Luther, Calvin; today, for example, Schreiner).
The whole law, but especially as it marked Jews off from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws, Sabbath (Dunn, Wright).
The ceremonial law only (Origen and Jerome, as Calvin reports). Calvin rejected this as too narrow.

faith.d: Trust in God and his promises, above all trust in Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. In the New Testament faith is not a meritorious work that earns salvation, but the empty hand that receives it (Romans 4:4–5). True faith is never idle: it ‘expresses itself through love’ (Galatians 5:6).

v.t: Saving faith is itself a gift of God, worked by the Spirit in those he calls (Westminster Confession 14.1).
Faith is made possible by God’s grace, which goes before it, but it is a real human response that a person could refuse. God has appointed faith as the condition of salvation.

righteousness.d: Being right with God, measured by his standard. In Paul it can mean God’s own faithfulness to do what is right and to save (Romans 3:21–26), or the right standing God gives to those who believe (Philippians 3:9). Abraham ‘believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Genesis 15:6; Galatians 3:6).

election.d: God’s choosing of people for salvation and for his purposes. Scripture plainly teaches that God chooses (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:29–30). Christians differ over the basis of that choice.

v.t: Before creation God freely chose particular people to be saved in Christ, ‘without any foresight of faith, or good works’ in them (Westminster Confession 3.5). His grace then brings them to faith.

God chose to save all who would believe in Christ (Remonstrance, art. 1). His choosing of individuals rests on his foreknowledge of their faith; or election is mainly the choice of a people, the church in Christ, which individuals join by faith.
Both affirm God’s predestining grace while insisting on genuine human freedom to cooperate or resist. Catholic theology contains a range of views on how the two fit together.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 3

atonement.d: How Christ’s death reconciles sinners to God (‘at-one-ment’). The New Testament uses several pictures for it: sacrifice, ransom, redemption, bearing the curse, victory over evil powers. Christians hold these together.

v.t: At its centre is penal substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty our sins deserved (Galatians 3:13; Isaiah 53:5).

Most also affirm that Christ died in our place, for every person, though only believers receive the benefit (Remonstrance, art. 2). Some prefer to describe it as satisfying God’s moral government of the world.
Orthodox theology characteristically puts the emphasis on Christ’s victory over sin, death and the devil, and the healing of human nature, rather than on legal categories.

src.l: The Five Arminian Articles (Remonstrance, 1610), in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 3

redemption.d: Being set free by the payment of a price, like a slave bought out of slavery. Christ ‘redeemed us from the curse of the law’ (Galatians 3:13), and ‘those under the law’ (4:5), at the cost of his own life.

covenant.d: A binding relationship established by God with promises and obligations: with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and the ‘new covenant’ in Christ (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20). In Galatians Paul sets the promise-covenant with Abraham, fulfilled in Christ, against the Sinai covenant as a way of standing before God.

v.t: Reads the whole Bible through the covenants. Many Reformed theologians speak of one ‘covenant of grace’ running through the Old and New Testaments in different forms.
Stresses clearer distinctions between God’s dealings with Israel and with the church.

law.d: Usually the law of Moses, the commands given at Sinai (Exodus–Deuteronomy). Sometimes it means the books of Moses as Scripture (Galatians 4:21). Paul calls it ‘holy, righteous and good’ (Romans 7:12) but insists it cannot give life or justify a sinner.

v.t: Traditionally distinguishes moral, ceremonial and civil law. The ceremonies are fulfilled in Christ; the moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, still guides Christian life (Westminster Confession ch. 19).
Stresses the contrast between law (what God demands, which exposes sin) and gospel (what God gives in Christ).

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 19

adoption.d: God’s act of making believers his children and heirs (Galatians 4:5; Romans 8:15). In Roman law an adopted son had full rights of inheritance. Believers share in the Son’s own relationship with the Father, and the Spirit leads them to call God ‘Abba, Father’.

perseverance.d: Whether a true believer will certainly continue in faith to the end, or can fall away and be lost. Scripture contains both strong promises of God keeping his people (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6) and serious warnings (Galatians 5:4; Hebrews 6:4–6).

v.t: Those truly united to Christ ‘can neither totally nor finally fall away’ but will be kept to the end (Westminster Confession 17.1). The warnings are real means God uses to keep them.
A true believer can turn from Christ and be finally lost (Wesley). The Remonstrance of 1610 left the question open; later Arminians generally affirmed the possibility.
Grace can be lost through grave (‘mortal’) sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance (Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 14).

flesh.d: In Paul’s moral sense, not the physical body but human nature turned in on itself and away from God (Galatians 5:16–21; Romans 8:5–8). Sometimes it simply means ordinary human life or descent (Galatians 2:20; 4:23).

sanctification.d: Being made holy. In one sense believers are already set apart for God (1 Corinthians 6:11). In another they are being changed, by the Spirit, into the likeness of Christ throughout life (2 Corinthians 3:18).

v.t: Sanctification always follows justification but is distinct from it, and remains imperfect in this life (Westminster Confession ch. 13).
Holds out the hope of ‘entire sanctification’ or ‘Christian perfection’ in this life: a heart wholly filled with love for God and neighbour. It is not freedom from all mistakes.
Sanctification is part of justification itself, the inner renewal of the person by grace.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 13

son-of-man.d: In Hebrew and Aramaic, ‘son of man’ ordinarily means ‘a human being’ (as often in Ezekiel and Psalm 8:4). In Daniel 7:13 ‘one like a son of man’ comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus used ‘the Son of Man’ as his main title for himself, both of his humble mission and suffering (Mark 10:45) and of his coming glory (Mark 14:62). It holds together his real humanity and his divine authority.

apocalyptic.d: From the Greek for ‘revelation’ or ‘unveiling’. It is a type of writing in which hidden heavenly realities and the future are revealed, often through visions, symbolic beasts and numbers, and angelic interpreters. Examples include Daniel 7–12, Revelation, and many Jewish writings of the period between the Testaments. Its symbols are meant to be decoded, not read literally, and its main message is that God is in control and will bring history to its goal.

antichrist.d: The word appears only in 1 and 2 John, of a coming opponent of Christ and of the many ‘antichrists’ already present (1 John 2:18). Christians have long linked it with Daniel’s little horn and final king, Paul’s ‘man of lawlessness’ (2 Thessalonians 2), and the beast of Revelation 13.

v.t: A single, final, personal enemy of God who will appear before Christ’s return (common among premillennial and dispensational Christians, and held by many others).

The principle of opposition to Christ embodied in many figures and powers through history, possibly culminating in a final one (many amillennial interpreters). The Reformers often identified Antichrist with the papacy; that view is now rare outside some confessional traditions.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

messiah.d: Hebrew mashiach, Greek christos: ‘anointed one’. In the Old Testament kings and priests were anointed with oil for their office. The prophets came to promise one coming king from David’s line who would rule for ever. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as this Messiah, the Christ.

resurrection.d: Being raised bodily from death to life. Daniel 12:2 is the clearest Old Testament statement of a future resurrection of the dead to one of two destinies. Jesus’ own bodily resurrection is the centre of the Christian faith and the pattern and guarantee of the resurrection of his people (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). It is affirmed by all historic Christian creeds (‘the resurrection of the body’).

wrath.d: God’s settled, holy opposition to sin and evil. It is not a loss of temper, but the response of a good God to what destroys his creation and his creatures. Paul speaks of it as both present (Romans 1:18) and future (2:5), and of Christ rescuing believers from it (5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

sin.d: Falling short of God’s glory and breaking his law (Romans 3:23; 1 John 3:4). It is both acts we commit and a power or condition that enslaves (Romans 6; 7:14). At root it is refusing to honour God as God and putting created things in his place (Romans 1:21–25).

propitiation.d: The Greek hilastērion (Romans 3:25) and related words (1 John 2:2; 4:10). In the Greek Old Testament it is the ‘mercy seat’ on the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. ‘Propitiation’ means turning away wrath; ‘expiation’ means wiping away sin.

v.t: Christ’s death is a propitiation: it satisfies God’s justice and turns away his wrath from those who believe, because Christ bore the penalty in their place.
Prefer expiation, or the ‘mercy seat’ picture, stressing that God himself provides the means of dealing with sin. Many hold that both ideas are present.

imputation.d: Crediting something to someone’s account (Greek logizomai, ‘to count’, ‘to credit’; Romans 4). Abraham’s faith was ‘credited to him as righteousness’.

v.t: Three imputations: Adam’s sin to his descendants, believers’ sin to Christ, and Christ’s righteousness to believers (Westminster Confession 6.3; 11.1).
Strongly affirms that Christ’s righteousness is credited to the believer through faith.
Affirms that believers are justified freely for Christ’s sake, with faith counted for righteousness; often more cautious about saying Christ’s active obedience itself is transferred.
Holds that justification includes a righteousness actually given to, and at work in, the believer, not only credited.

original-sin.d: The effect of the first sin of Adam on the whole human race: all are born into a condition of sinfulness and death (Romans 5:12–21; Psalm 51:5). All historic Christian traditions affirm that humanity is fallen; they differ on whether Adam’s guilt itself is passed on.

v.t: Adam’s guilt is imputed to all his descendants, and a corrupted nature is passed on (Westminster Confession 6.3).
Original sin is ‘contracted’, not ‘committed’: the loss of original holiness and a wounded nature inclined to sin, taken away in baptism (Catechism 404–405).
Speaks of ‘ancestral sin’: all inherit death and corruption from Adam, but not his personal guilt.
Affirms a corrupted nature that cannot turn to God without grace; views differ on inherited guilt.

reconciliation.d: The restoring of a broken relationship (Greek katallassō). Through Christ’s death God reconciles to himself people who were his enemies (Romans 5:10–11; 2 Corinthians 5:18–21). It is God who takes the initiative.

incarnation.d: God the Son becoming fully human (‘the Word became flesh’, John 1:14), without ceasing to be God. Christians confess one person, Jesus Christ, with two complete natures, divine and human, neither mixed nor divided (Definition of Chalcedon, AD 451). This is shared ground for Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians alike.

trinity.d: The one God exists eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet there is only one God. The word is not in the Bible, but the church found the truth there: one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), the Father is God, the Son is God (John 1:1; 20:28), the Spirit is God (Acts 5:3–4), and the three are distinct (Matthew 28:19). Confessed in the Nicene Creed (AD 325/381) by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches. Jehovah’s Witnesses and some other groups reject it.

src.l: Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), in Schaff vol. 2

regeneration.d: The work of the Holy Spirit giving new spiritual life to a person, so that they are ‘born again’ or ‘born from above’ (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5). All agree it is God’s work, not human achievement. They differ on how it relates to faith and baptism.

v.t: The Spirit gives new life first, and as a result the person believes. Regeneration is God’s sovereign act, which people cannot cause or resist (Westminster Confession 10.1–2).
God’s ‘prevenient’ grace, going before, enables every person to respond; the new birth follows faith. Wesley saw baptism as its ‘outward sign and means’, ‘wherever baptism can be had’.
God ordinarily gives the new birth through baptism. The Catholic Catechism says baptism ‘signifies and actually brings about the birth of water and the Spirit’ (1215).
